Chapter 1 · Understanding Computer Systems

Understanding Computer Systems

Chapter 1 — Understanding Computer Systems

Learning objectives

- Define a computer system - Identify its major elements - Describe the information-processing cycle. What is a Computer System? A computer system is an arrangement of hardware and software that accepts data, processes it according to instructions, stores information, and produces results. The familiar input–process–output model is useful, but storage and communication are also essential parts of modern computing. Hardware refers to physical components: processor, memory, storage, motherboard, display, and peripherals. Software consists of programs and instructions. Data is the material that programs process. People, procedures, and networks complete the wider system context. For example, when a student edits a document, the keyboard supplies input, the CPU executes application instructions, RAM holds active data, storage preserves the file, and the display presents the result. Each part has a distinct responsibility, yet none works alone.

1.1 The Information-Processing Cycle The information-processing cycle is commonly described through

four functions: input, processing, output, and storage. Input devices convert actions or measurements into machine-readable data. Processing transforms that data using instructions. Output devices present results in a form people or other systems can use. Storage retains programs and data for later use. A point-of-sale terminal illustrates the cycle. A scanner reads a product code, the processor and software look up the item, a display shows its price, and a database or local storage records the transaction. Network communication may connect the terminal to a central service.

Chapter 1 · Understanding Computer Systems

Understanding Computer Systems

The cycle is not always strictly sequential. Systems often overlap input, computation, storage, and output to improve responsiveness. A video player, for instance, receives network packets while decoding frames and sending audio and images to output devices.

1.2 Hardware and Software

Hardware and software are complementary. Hardware provides physical resources; software directs those resources toward tasks. System software manages the machine and offers common services. Application software supports user goals such as writing, communication, design, and analysis. Firmware is software stored in nonvolatile memory and used for low-level control or initialization. Device drivers allow an operating system to communicate with specific hardware. Utilities perform maintenance, monitoring, backup, or security functions. A useful way to understand the relationship is to follow an application request. The application asks the operating system to save a file. The operating system uses a file-system service and storage driver. The controller then transfers data to a storage device. This layered cooperation makes it possible for applications to work across many hardware models.

1.3 System Boundaries and Interfaces A system boundary defines which components are considered part of the system being studied

A laptop can be examined as a single computer, or as a client in a network service. In a broader view, its platform includes the processor architecture, operating system, drivers, libraries, and supported application environment. An interface is a defined point of interaction between components. Hardware interfaces include connectors and electrical signaling. Software interfaces include APIs, system

Chapter 2 · Computer System Platforms

Computer System Platforms

calls, and instruction sets. Clear interfaces allow components to be changed independently when compatibility is preserved. When studying a system, identify its purpose, inputs, outputs, internal components, and external connections. This habit helps avoid treating a complex computer as one mysterious object. Chapter 1 Review and Activity

Review questions

1. What is a computer system? 2. How do hardware and software differ? 3. Name the four functions in the information-processing cycle. 4. What is firmware? 5. Why are interfaces important? Activity Choose a familiar device—laptop, smartphone, ATM, or game console. Create a labeled diagram showing at least five hardware components and three software layers. Trace one user action through input, processing, storage or communication, and output.

Key idea A computer system is a coordinated set of components. Understanding the connections among components is more important than memorizing a list of parts.

Chapter 2 — Computer System Platforms A computer system platform is the combination of hardware, system software, and interfaces that supports the execution of applications. The term may refer to a device family, processor architecture, operating system environment, or complete deployment environment. Examples include a Windows desktop using an x86-64 processor, an Android phone using an ARM-based system-on-chip, a Linux server, a game console, and a microcontroller board. These platforms differ in performance, energy use, cost, available interfaces, and intended workload.

Chapter 2 · Computer System Platforms

Computer System Platforms

Platform selection should begin with requirements. Consider what applications must run, how much processing and memory are needed, what peripherals are required, how the system will be maintained, and what security constraints apply.

2.1 Platform Layers A platform can be viewed as a stack of layers

At the bottom are electronic components and physical interconnects. Above them are processor architecture and firmware. The operating system manages resources and exposes services. Libraries and runtime environments provide reusable capabilities. Applications use these services to perform user tasks. Layers reduce complexity by defining responsibilities. An application does not need to control every electrical signal in a processor. It requests a service through an API, and lower layers handle implementation details. However, abstraction has limits. Performance, device compatibility, and security can depend on details below the application layer. Platform knowledge helps developers make informed choices without needing to understand every transistor.

2.2 Platform Compatibility Compatibility describes whether software, hardware, or data can work correctly in a particular environment

Source-code compatibility means code can be built with suitable tools. Binary compatibility means an existing compiled program can run without being rebuilt, provided the platform contract is met. Data compatibility concerns whether formats can be read and interpreted. Compatibility may depend on processor instruction set, operating-system APIs, runtime version, libraries, drivers, and application configuration. A program built for one operating system may not run directly on another even if both use the same CPU family. Portable software reduces platform-specific assumptions. Standards, documented APIs, managed runtimes, and cross-platform frameworks can help, though testing is still necessary.

2.3 Choosing a Platform Platform choice is a trade-off rather than a search for one universally best computer

A mobile device prioritizes battery life, compact size, and integrated sensors. A workstation emphasizes high performance and expandability. A server prioritizes throughput, availability, remote management, and data protection. An embedded controller may prioritize predictable timing, low cost, and low power.

Chapter 3 · Computer Architecture and Organization

Computer Architecture and Organization

A basic decision matrix can compare requirements such as cost, performance, energy, reliability, software support, security, and upgradeability. Assign importance to each requirement and evaluate candidate platforms against evidence. Scenario: A small school library needs a catalog application and reliable backups. The best platform may be a modest server or managed cloud service rather than a high-end gaming computer. Chapter 2 Review and Activity

Review questions

1. What does the term platform include? 2. Give three examples of computing platforms. 3. Explain the difference between binary and source compatibility. 4. Why do platform requirements differ by workload? 5. What factors belong in a platform decision matrix? Activity Compare a laptop, smartphone, and single-board computer. Make a table of processor family, operating system, memory, typical power source, I/O features, and suitable uses. State which device best fits a selected task and explain your decision.

Chapter 3 — Computer Architecture and Organization Computer architecture describes the attributes of a system that are visible to a programmer, including instructions, registers, data types, and memory addressing. Computer organization describes how those architectural features are implemented through hardware components and control mechanisms. Two processors may implement the same instruction set architecture (ISA) while differing in pipeline depth, cache size, execution units, or manufacturing technology. Software can remain compatible even as organization changes. This distinction is central to platform design. Architecture defines a contract; organization determines how efficiently the system fulfills it. The contract includes instruction behavior, register semantics, and memory rules.

3.1 Architecture, Organization, and Implementation Architecture, organization, and implementation are related but distinct

Architecture defines what a machine exposes. The organization explains how functional units are

Chapter 3 · Computer Architecture and Organization

Computer Architecture and Organization

arranged and coordinated. Implementation concerns the physical realization, such as transistor technology, circuit layout, and fabrication process. For example, an ISA may define an integer addition instruction. The organization may use a pipelined arithmetic logic unit to execute it. Implementation determines the circuitry, timing, and physical characteristics of that unit. These distinctions support fair comparisons. A benchmark result is influenced by architecture, organization, implementation, software, and workload. No single specification such as clock frequency fully describes system performance.

3.2 Von Neumann and Harvard Concepts

The stored-program concept places instructions and data in memory so that a processor can fetch and execute programs. A traditional Von Neumann model uses a shared memory path for instructions and data. A Harvard model uses separate instruction and data memories or pathways. Many modern processors use a modified Harvard arrangement internally while presenting a unified memory model to software. A shared path can simplify design but may create contention when instruction fetch and data access compete. Separate paths can increase throughput for particular workloads. Real systems combine techniques to balance flexibility, performance, and cost.

Chapter 4 · Data Representation and Number Systems

Data Representation and Number Systems

The important lesson is that memory organization affects how quickly the processor can obtain both instructions and operands.

3.3 System-Level Architecture A complete computer includes more than a CPU

The processor communicates with memory, storage, graphics, network interfaces, and other devices through interconnects and controllers. Firmware initializes the platform, while the operating system manages resources after startup. System-level architecture defines how these components connect and how responsibilities are divided. Modern systems may integrate several components into one chip, but their logical functions remain recognizable. When analyzing a system diagram, trace the path of data. Ask where it originates, which component transforms it, how it moves, where it is stored, and which component ultimately presents it. Chapter 3 Review and Activity

Review questions

1. Define computer architecture. 2. How does organization differ from architecture? 3. What is an ISA? 4. Compare the basic Von Neumann and Harvard concepts. 5. Why is clock speed alone not enough to compare processors? Activity Draw a block diagram of a computer system. Include CPU, main memory, storage, input/output, and system interconnect. Use arrows to indicate data movement and annotate each component’s role.

Chapter 4 — Data Representation and Number Systems Digital systems represent information using discrete states, commonly described as binary 0 and 1. A bit is one binary digit. A group of eight bits is a byte. Larger quantities are measured using units such as kilobytes, megabytes, gigabytes, and tebibytes; decimal and binary prefixes should not be confused.

Chapter 4 · Data Representation and Number Systems

Data Representation and Number Systems

Binary representation is fundamental because electronic circuits can reliably distinguish two states. Numbers, text, images, audio, and instructions are encoded into bit patterns according to defined formats. A bit pattern has no universal meaning by itself. Interpretation depends on context: the same bits may represent an integer, a character, a color channel, or an instruction.

4.1 Binary, Decimal, and Hexadecimal

The decimal system uses ten digits and powers of ten. Binary uses two digits and powers of two. Hexadecimal uses sixteen symbols—0 through 9 and A through F—and provides a compact way to write binary values because each hexadecimal digit corresponds to four bits. Example: binary 1010 1111 equals hexadecimal AF. The left nibble 1010 represents A (decimal 10), and 1111 represents F (decimal 15). Hexadecimal is common in memory addresses, machine code, and debugging tools. Practice converting values in both directions. Group binary digits in fours when converting to hexadecimal, and expand each hexadecimal digit into four bits when converting back.

4.2 Signed and Unsigned Integers An unsigned n-bit integer can represent values from 0 through 2ⁿ−1

A signed two’s-complement n-bit integer commonly represents values from −2ⁿ⁻¹ through 2ⁿ⁻¹−1. Two’s complement makes addition and subtraction efficient in digital hardware. For eight bits, unsigned values range from 0 to 255, while signed two’s-complement values range from −128 to 127. Overflow occurs when a mathematical result cannot be represented in the selected width. Programs must handle overflow according to language and system rules. When examining data, always identify its width and signedness. A bit pattern alone does not reveal the intended numerical interpretation.

4.3 Characters, Images, and Audio

Chapter 5 · Digital Logic and System Components

Digital Logic and System Components

Text is represented using character encodings. Unicode defines a broad character set, while UTF-8 is a widely used variable-length encoding. Images are commonly represented as pixels with color components; resolution and bit depth influence storage requirements. Audio is represented through sampling and quantization, where sample rate and bit depth affect fidelity and data size. Compression reduces storage or transmission size. Lossless compression preserves the original data exactly. Lossy compression discards selected information to achieve greater reduction, often used for photographs, audio, and video. The choice of representation influences memory needs, bandwidth, quality, and processing cost. Chapter 4 Review and Activity

Review questions

1. What is a bit and a byte? 2. Why is hexadecimal useful? 3. What is the range of an unsigned n-bit integer? 4. Explain two’s-complement representation. 5. Compare lossless and lossy compression. Activity Convert decimal 37 to binary and hexadecimal. Explain how an image’s resolution and color depth affect its memory size. Identify one example of a lossless and one lossy format.

Chapter 5 — Digital Logic and System Components Digital logic circuits process binary signals. Basic gates include AND, OR, NOT, NAND, NOR, XOR, and XNOR. Combinational circuits produce outputs based on current inputs. Sequential circuits also depend on stored state, usually represented by flip-flops or registers. These building blocks form arithmetic units, control circuits, counters, memory cells, and interfaces. The system’s behavior emerges from the coordinated operation of many small circuits. Understanding logic helps explain how high-level operations are ultimately implemented by electronic hardware.

Chapter 5 · Digital Logic and System Components

Digital Logic and System Components

5.1 Logic Gates and Truth Tables

A truth table lists the output of a logic function for every possible input combination. An AND gate outputs 1 only when all inputs are 1. An OR gate outputs 1 when at least one input is 1. NOT reverses a single input. XOR outputs 1 when its inputs differ. NAND and NOR are functionally complete: circuits can be built using only one of these gate types. XOR is useful in arithmetic and parity operations. Logic simplification can reduce circuit complexity, power, and delay. Truth tables provide a systematic way to verify logic. For n binary inputs, there are 2ⁿ possible combinations.

5.2 Combinational and Sequential Circuits A combinational circuit has no internal memory of prior input values

Examples include multiplexers, decoders, adders, and comparators. A sequential circuit stores state and

Chapter 6 · The Central Processing Unit

The Central Processing Unit

may use a clock to coordinate changes. Examples include registers, counters, and finite-state machines. A register stores a group of bits. A clock defines timing events for synchronous circuits. Setup and hold requirements describe when data must be stable around a clock edge. Violating timing requirements can lead to unreliable behavior. The CPU relies on both types: combinational logic computes results, while sequential elements preserve instructions, operands, and control state.

5.3 From Logic to a System A processor’s arithmetic logic unit uses circuits to perform operations s

uch as addition, subtraction, bitwise logic, and comparisons. Control logic selects operations and coordinates data movement. Registers store values close to the execution units. Interconnects move signals among components. At the system level, logic circuits are packaged into integrated circuits and connected through a motherboard or system-on-chip. Designers must consider timing, power, heat, manufacturing constraints, and fault behavior. This progression—from gates to functional units to complete systems—shows how architecture becomes physical hardware. Chapter 5 Review and Activity

Review questions

1. What does an AND gate do? 2. How does a sequential circuit differ from a combinational circuit? 3. What is a register? 4. Why is clock timing important? 5. Name three functions of an ALU. Activity: Create truth tables for AND, OR, NOT, and XOR. Then sketch a simple block diagram showing how registers, an ALU, and control logic cooperate during an arithmetic operation.

Chapter 6 — The Central Processing Unit The central processing unit (CPU) executes instructions and coordinates much of a computer’s activity. Its principal elements include registers, execution units, control logic, and interfaces to memory and other components.

Chapter 6 · The Central Processing Unit

The Central Processing Unit

The CPU repeatedly obtains instructions, interprets them, and performs the specified operations. Modern processors improve throughput using pipelines, multiple execution units, branch prediction, and other techniques. These techniques must preserve the architectural behavior expected by software. A CPU is not the whole computer. Its performance depends on memory, storage, software, cooling, and workload characteristics.

6.1 Registers and the ALU

Registers are small, fast storage locations inside the processor. General-purpose registers hold operands and results. Special-purpose registers may track instruction location, status flags, stack information, or control state. The exact set is defined by the architecture. The arithmetic logic unit performs integer arithmetic and logical operations. Floating-point units handle operations on floating-point values. Some processors include specialized units for vector processing, cryptography, or machine learning. Keeping frequently used values in registers reduces the need to access slower memory. Compiler register allocation is therefore an important part of generating efficient machine code.

6.2 Clock, Cores, and Threads A processor clock provides timing references for synchronous operation

Clock frequency is measured in cycles per second, but one cycle does not necessarily equal one completed instruction. Different instructions may require different resources and numbers of cycles.

Chapter 6 · The Central Processing Unit

The Central Processing Unit

A multicore processor contains multiple processing cores. A hardware thread is an execution context supported by a core; some cores support more than one thread concurrently. Parallelism can improve performance when software has work that can be divided and coordinated. More cores do not automatically make every application faster. Serial work, synchronization, memory bandwidth, and software design limit the benefits.

6.3 CPU Performance CPU performance depends on instruction count, cycles per instruction (CPI), and clock frequency

A simplified relationship is CPU time = instruction count × CPI × cycle time. This model helps explain why reducing instructions, improving execution efficiency, or increasing frequency can affect runtime. Real systems add complications: cache misses, branch behavior, power limits, thermal throttling, and operating-system scheduling. Benchmarks should represent the workload of interest and be interpreted carefully. Performance optimization should begin with measurement. A faster component may not improve total runtime if another component is the bottleneck. Chapter 6 Review and Activity

Review questions

1. What are the main CPU components? 2. What is the purpose of a register? 3. How do cores differ from hardware threads? 4. Why is clock frequency not a complete performance measure? 5. What factors influence CPU time? Activity: Select two computing tasks, such as video editing and web browsing. Identify which CPU features may matter most for each and explain why workload characteristics affect performance.

Chapter 7 · Instruction Set Architecture

Instruction Set Architecture

Chapter 7 — Instruction Set Architecture An instruction set architecture (ISA) is the interface between software and processor hardware. It defines machine instructions, registers, data types, addressing modes, and architectural behavior. The ISA allows software tools to target a consistent machine model. Common ISA families include x86-64, ARM, and RISC-V. Each has its own instruction encoding and architectural conventions. The ISA alone does not specify every implementation detail, so processors with the same ISA can have different performance and power characteristics. Compilers translate high-level language programs into machine instructions supported by a target ISA.

7.1 Instruction Formats and Operations Machine instructions encode operations and information such a

s register identifiers, immediate values, or memory addresses. Common operation categories include data transfer, arithmetic, logical operations, control flow, and system instructions. An instruction format determines how bits are divided into fields. Fixed-length formats can simplify instruction decoding, while variable-length formats can improve code density but may add decoding complexity. Architectures make different trade-offs. Assembly language gives human-readable names to machine instructions. It is useful for learning processor behavior, debugging, and examining compiler output.

7.2 Addressing Modes Addressing modes specify how an instruction identifies its operands

Immediate addressing embeds a value in the instruction. Register addressing uses a register. Direct or absolute addressing identifies a memory location. Indirect addressing uses a register or memory value to locate an operand. Base-plus-offset addressing is common for arrays and structures. For example, an instruction that loads from address base register plus offset can access a field within a data structure. The ISA defines the exact semantics and limits of such addressing. Addressing modes influence code size, flexibility, and instruction complexity.

Chapter 8 · The Instruction Cycle and Control

The Instruction Cycle and Control

7.3 RISC and CISC Concepts Reduced Instruction Set Computer (RISC) designs traditionally emphasize r

elatively simple instructions and regular formats. Complex Instruction Set Computer (CISC) designs traditionally provide a richer set of instruction forms. These are broad historical categories, not absolute descriptions of every modern processor. Modern implementations often combine ideas. A complex instruction may be decoded into simpler internal operations, while a RISC design may include specialized instructions. Performance depends on the complete implementation and software workload. The key distinction for students is that the ISA is a software-visible contract, while internal execution can be much more sophisticated. Chapter 7 Review and Activity

Review questions

1. What does ISA stand for? 2. Why can processors with the same ISA differ in performance? 3. Name four instruction categories. 4. Explain immediately and register addressing. 5. Describe the general RISC and CISC concepts. Activity Write a short pseudocode sequence to add two values and store the result. Identify the kinds of machine instructions a compiler might use, such as loads, addition, and store.

Chapter 8 — The Instruction Cycle and Control The instruction cycle describes the repeated steps used to execute program instructions. A simplified cycle includes fetch, decode, operand access, execute, memory access when needed, and write-back. The exact stages differ among processor designs. Control logic coordinates these actions. It selects registers, directs data paths, chooses ALU operations, and manages instruction sequencing. Control can be implemented through hardwired logic, microcode, or a combination. Modern CPUs overlap stages through pipelining. The simple instruction-cycle model remains useful for understanding the fundamental work performed.

Chapter 8 · The Instruction Cycle and Control

The Instruction Cycle and Control

8.1 Fetch and Decode During fetch, the processor obtains an instruction from memory, often using a p

rogram counter or instruction pointer. The processor updates the pointer according to the instruction sequence or control-flow behavior. During decode, the instruction’s operation and operands are identified. Instruction fetch can be accelerated by instruction caches and prefetch mechanisms. Decoding can be complex when instruction formats vary. A decoded instruction may be represented internally in a form suitable for execution units. If an instruction changes control flow, the next instruction address may differ from the sequential address.

8.2 Execute, Memory, and Write-Back During execution, an ALU or other functional unit performs the operation

A load or store instruction may access data memory. A result is written to a destination register or other architectural location when the instruction completes. A branch instruction evaluates a condition and selects a target address. Exceptions and interrupts can redirect execution to system handling routines. The architecture defines the visible behavior, while the organization determines the detailed mechanism. These stages are conceptual. A real processor may fuse, split, reorder, or overlap operations internally while maintaining required program behavior.

8.3 Pipelining and Hazards Pipelining divides instruction processing into stages so multiple instructions can be in progress at once

Ideally, after the pipeline fills, one instruction completes per cycle. Actual throughput depends on stage balance and hazards. A structural hazard occurs when instructions compete for a resource. A data hazard occurs when an instruction depends on a result not yet available. A control hazard occurs when the next instruction depends on a branch decision. Techniques such as forwarding, stalls, scheduling, and prediction help manage hazards.

Chapter 9 · Memory Systems and Hierarchy

Memory Systems and Hierarchy

Pipeline depth is a design trade-off. Deeper pipelines may support higher frequency but can increase penalties when execution must be redirected. Chapter 8 Review and Activity

Review questions

1. List the basic instruction-cycle stages. 2. What does the control unit do? 3. Explain instruction pipelining. 4. Compare structural, data, and control hazards. 5. Why can a branch disrupt a pipeline? Activity Draw a five-stage pipeline and show how three instructions overlap. Mark one possible data hazard and describe a forwarding or stall solution.

Chapter 9 — Memory Systems and Hierarchy Computer memory stores instructions and data needed by the processor. Memory technologies differ in capacity, speed, cost per bit, and persistence. A memory hierarchy places small, fast storage near the CPU and larger, slower storage farther away. Registers, cache, main memory, and secondary storage form a typical hierarchy. The hierarchy works because programs often exhibit locality: recently used or nearby data is likely to be used again. The system designer seeks a balance. Fast memory is expensive and limited, while large storage is more affordable but slower to access.

9.1 RAM and ROM

Random Access Memory (RAM) provides read/write storage used by active programs and data. DRAM is commonly used for main memory because it offers high density and reasonable cost, but it requires periodic refreshing. SRAM is faster and does not require refresh, making it useful for caches, though it is more expensive per bit.

Chapter 9 · Memory Systems and Hierarchy

Memory Systems and Hierarchy

Read-only memory (ROM) and related nonvolatile technologies preserve information without power. Firmware may be stored in flash memory. The term ROM is sometimes used broadly for memory that is not intended for ordinary application writes. Volatile memory loses its contents when power is removed. Nonvolatile memory retains data across power loss.

9.2 Memory Hierarchy and Locality Temporal locality means recently accessed data is likely to be accessed again

Spatial locality means addresses near a recently accessed location are likely to be used soon. Caches exploit both patterns by keeping selected blocks closer to the processor. A typical hierarchy includes registers, L1 cache, L2 cache, L3 cache, DRAM, and persistent storage. Not every system has all levels or uses the same organization. Access time generally increases as capacity grows and distance from the CPU increases. Programs with good locality often perform better because they reduce expensive lower-level accesses.

9.3 Memory Access and Bandwidth Latency is the time required to complete an access

Bandwidth is the amount of data transferred per unit time. A memory system can have high bandwidth but still exhibit significant latency for an individual request. Multiple channels, wider interfaces, burst transfers, and parallel requests can increase bandwidth. Workloads that stream large arrays may be bandwidth-bound, while workloads with dependent pointer accesses may be latency-bound. Memory performance should be evaluated using the pattern of access, not only the advertised transfer rate. Chapter 9 Review and Activity

Review questions

Chapter 10 · Cache and Virtual Memory

Cache and Virtual Memory

1. What is the role of main memory? 2. Compare SRAM and DRAM. 3. Explain temporal and spatial locality. 4. How does latency differ from bandwidth? 5. Why is a memory hierarchy useful? Activity Draw a memory pyramid and label each level with typical relative capacity, speed, and cost. Explain where a currently running application’s instructions and data may reside.

Chapter 10 — Cache and Virtual Memory Caches reduce average memory access time by storing copies of recently or frequently used data. A cache hit occurs when the requested block is present. A miss requires retrieving the block from a lower level. Hit rate and miss penalty strongly influence performance. Virtual memory gives each process an address space that is mapped to physical memory. It supports isolation, flexible allocation, and the ability to use storage as backing for pages not currently resident in RAM. Hardware memory-management units and operating-system software cooperate to implement these mechanisms.

10.1 Cache Organization A cache is organized into lines or blocks

Address bits identify a block offset, a set or index, and a tag. Direct-mapped caches place each memory block in one possible location. Set-associative caches allow a block to occupy one of several ways within a set. Fully associative caches allow placement anywhere, but require more complex lookup. Replacement policies choose which line to evict when space is needed. Write-through caches propagate writes to the next level, while write-back caches may retain modified data until eviction. Each choice affects complexity, traffic, and performance. Cache coherence becomes important when multiple cores maintain copies of shared data.

10.2 Virtual Address Translation

Chapter 11 · Input and Output Systems

Input and Output Systems

A program uses virtual addresses. The memory-management unit translates them into physical addresses using page tables and translation lookaside buffers (TLBs). A TLB caches recent translations to avoid repeated page-table walks. Memory is commonly divided into fixed-size pages and frames. The operating system maps virtual pages to physical frames and controls permissions. A page fault occurs when a referenced page is not currently mapped in a way that permits the access; the operating system then handles the condition. Virtual memory provides isolation, but excessive page faults and swapping can severely reduce performance.

10.3 Protection and Sharing Virtual memory allows processes to have separate address spaces

Page permissions can restrict reading, writing, or executing selected regions. Shared pages can allow processes to use common libraries or communicate efficiently when designed safely. Isolation helps prevent one application from directly corrupting another application’s memory. It is not a complete security solution: vulnerabilities in the operating system, drivers, or hardware may still create risks. Memory protection is a foundational platform feature that supports reliability, security, and controlled resource sharing. Chapter 10 Review and Activity

Review questions

1. What is a cache hit and a cache miss? 2. Compare direct-mapped and set-associative caches. 3. What is virtual memory? 4. What does a TLB store? 5. How does page protection support isolation? Activity Use a simple address example to identify page number and page offset. Explain how a TLB hit differs from a page-table walk, and describe why excessive page faults slow a system.

Chapter 11 — Input and Output Systems

Chapter 11 · Input and Output Systems

Input and Output Systems

Input/output (I/O) systems connect a computer to external devices such as keyboards, displays, storage, sensors, printers, and network interfaces. Devices differ in speed, data format, and control requirements. The operating system commonly uses device drivers and standard I/O interfaces to manage hardware differences. Applications can use familiar operations while drivers translate them into device-specific commands. I/O architecture must balance responsiveness, throughput, reliability, and safe sharing of devices.

11.1 Programmed I/O and Interrupts In programmed I/O, the CPU repeatedly checks device status or moves data through instructions

This method is simple but can waste processor time when a device is slow. Interrupt-driven I/O allows a device to notify the processor when attention is needed. An interrupt causes control to move to a handler that performs or schedules appropriate work. The system must preserve relevant state and ensure interrupt handling is safe and efficient. Interrupts improve utilization, but high interrupt rates or poorly designed handlers can create overhead.

11.2 Direct Memory Access Direct Memory Access (DMA) allows a device or controller to transfer data

between the device and memory with limited CPU involvement. The CPU configures the transfer, and the controller performs the movement. Completion may be reported through an interrupt. DMA is useful for high-volume transfers such as storage and networking. Correct operation requires careful coordination of memory ownership, buffers, and cache consistency. Operating systems and hardware provide mechanisms to manage these concerns. DMA can improve throughput and free CPU cycles, but it does not eliminate the need for drivers or system-level coordination.

Chapter 12 · Storage Technologies

Storage Technologies

11.3 Device Drivers and Interfaces A device driver is software that controls or communicates with a hardware device

Drivers may run in privileged operating-system space or in other supported execution contexts. A faulty driver can affect stability because it interacts closely with hardware and system resources. Standard interfaces help applications remain independent of specific devices. Plug-and-play mechanisms can identify hardware and load appropriate drivers. Device permissions and updates are important security considerations. When troubleshooting a device, check physical connections, power, operating-system recognition, driver status, and application configuration. Chapter 11 Review and Activity

Review questions

1. What is the purpose of an I/O system? 2. Compare programmed I/O and interrupt-driven I/O. 3. What is DMA? 4. Why are device drivers needed? 5. What risks can a faulty driver create? Activity Trace a file read from a storage device into an application’s memory. Identify the roles of the application, operating system, driver, controller, DMA if applicable, and CPU.

Chapter 12 — Storage Technologies Storage preserves data beyond the lifetime of a program or power session. Common technologies include hard disk drives (HDDs), solid-state drives (SSDs), removable flash storage, and network-based storage services. HDDs store data magnetically on rotating media and use mechanical movement. SSDs use flash memory and have no moving parts. Their performance, endurance, capacity, and cost characteristics differ. Storage selection depends on workload, budget, durability, and capacity requirements.

12.1 HDDs and SSDs

Chapter 12 · Storage Technologies

Storage Technologies

HDD performance is influenced by rotational delay, seek time, and transfer rate. SSDs typically provide much lower access latency because they avoid mechanical movement. However, flash memory has erase and write characteristics that require controllers to manage mapping, wear leveling, and garbage collection. SSD endurance is often described using measures such as total bytes written or drive writes per day. Actual lifespan depends on workload, device quality, and operating conditions. Backups remain necessary regardless of storage type. A practical platform may use an SSD for operating system and applications, with larger-capacity storage for archives.

12.2 File Systems A file system organizes stored data into files and directories and tracks metadata

such as names, sizes, permissions, and timestamps. It maps logical file operations to storage structures. Examples include NTFS, exFAT, ext4, APFS, and other file systems used in different environments. File systems may provide journaling, checksums, encryption, snapshots, or other features. These capabilities vary, and a feature’s presence does not replace a backup strategy.

Chapter 13 · Operating Systems and System Software

Operating Systems and System Software

File permissions and ownership help control access. File-system consistency tools may repair selected structural problems after an unexpected shutdown.

12.3 RAID and Backup Redundant Array of Independent Disks (RAID) combines storage devices to improve

performance, availability, or both. Different RAID levels use striping, mirroring, or parity in different ways. RAID is not a substitute for backup because it may not protect against accidental deletion, malware, theft, or site-wide damage. A backup is a separate copy of data that can be restored. A sound strategy considers frequency, retention, off-site or isolated copies, and regular restore testing. The value of a backup is demonstrated by successful recovery. Storage planning should include capacity, reliability, security, and recovery objectives. Chapter 12 Review and Activity

Review questions

1. How do HDDs and SSDs differ? 2. What is a file system? 3. What does RAID attempt to provide? 4. Why is RAID not a backup? 5. Why should restores be tested? Activity Design a storage plan for a student computer containing the operating system, applications, schoolwork, and backups. Explain the role of each storage location and how important files would be recovered.

Chapter 13 — Operating Systems and System Software An operating system (OS) manages hardware resources and provides services to applications. Major responsibilities include process management, memory management, file systems, device control, security, and user interaction. System software also includes firmware, drivers, utilities, libraries, and runtime environments. These layers allow application developers to work with stable interfaces rather than directly controlling every hardware component.

Chapter 13 · Operating Systems and System Software

Operating Systems and System Software

Examples of operating systems include Windows, Linux distributions, macOS, Android, and iOS. Their design goals and supported platforms vary.

13.1 Processes and Threads A process is an executing program with resources and an address space managed by the operating system

A thread is an execution path within a process. Threads in one process commonly share memory and resources, while separate processes are more strongly isolated. The scheduler selects which runnable thread or process receives CPU time. Context switching saves and restores execution state. Scheduling policies balance responsiveness, fairness, throughput, and priority requirements. Concurrency allows multiple tasks to make progress during overlapping periods. Parallelism means tasks execute at the same time on different execution resources. Shared-state concurrency requires careful synchronization.

13.2 Memory and File Management The operating system allocates memory, enforces protection, and coor

dinates virtual-to-physical mappings. It also manages files and directories, providing operations such as create, read, write, rename, and delete. File permissions and access controls determine who may perform operations. The OS may cache file data to improve performance. It must coordinate cached data with storage and maintain consistency according to system rules. Resource management is a central OS function: applications compete for CPU time, memory, storage, and I/O, and the system must allocate them safely.

13.3 System Calls and User Mode Applications usually run in user mode with restricted privileges

Operating-system kernels run with greater privilege and provide controlled access to protected resources. A system call is a defined transition through which an application requests a kernel service.

Chapter 14 · Buses and Interconnects

Buses and Interconnects

Examples include opening a file, creating a process, allocating memory, or communicating through a socket. The OS validates arguments and permissions before carrying out the operation. Privilege separation limits the damage that ordinary application code can cause. Secure platform design minimizes unnecessary privileged code and carefully validates transitions. Review questions

1. List five operating-system responsibilities. 2. Compare a process and a thread. 3. What does a scheduler do? 4. What is a system call? 5. Why do systems distinguish user mode and kernel mode? Activity Use an operating system’s task manager or process monitor. Identify several processes, observe CPU and memory usage, and explain how the OS shares resources among them.

Chapter 14 — Buses and Interconnects Interconnects provide communication paths among processors, memory, storage, and peripherals. A bus is a shared communication structure with defined signaling and protocol rules. Modern platforms may use point-to-point links, switched fabrics, and integrated on-chip networks. Interconnect characteristics include bandwidth, latency, topology, arbitration, and scalability. The design affects how efficiently components exchange data and how many devices can be supported. A system diagram should distinguish logical connections from physical connectors. A port visible to the user may connect through multiple internal controllers and links.

14.1 Bus Signals and Arbitration A traditional bus may include data, address, and control signals

The address identifies a destination, data carries information, and control signals define operations and timing.

Chapter 14 · Buses and Interconnects

Buses and Interconnects

Shared buses require arbitration when multiple devices request access at the same time. Arbitration policies may prioritize requests or distribute access fairly. A bottleneck can occur when aggregate demand exceeds the bus’s capacity. Modern architectures often use multiple links to reduce contention. Bus design is an example of a platform trade-off among simplicity, cost, throughput, and scalability.

14.2 PCI Express and USB PCI Express (PCIe) is a high-speed interconnect commonly used for graphics, storage, and expansion devices

It uses point-to-point links and lanes to provide scalable bandwidth. Generations and lane counts affect potential transfer rates; actual performance depends on implementation and workload. Universal Serial Bus (USB) supports a broad range of peripherals, including keyboards, storage devices, cameras, and docks. USB versions and connector types should not be confused: a connector’s physical shape does not alone establish supported speed or power features. Compatibility requires checking device, host, cable, and protocol capabilities.

14.3 System-on-Chip Interconnects A system-on-chip (SoC) integrates multiple functional components onto one semiconductor device

These may include CPU cores, graphics, memory controllers, media engines, I/O controllers, and AI accelerators. Internal interconnects coordinate communication among these units. Integration can reduce board space and energy for communication, but it also creates design challenges involving shared bandwidth, heat, and resource contention. Some SoCs use network-on-chip structures to connect many components. The system-level view remains valuable even when components are physically integrated. Chapter 14 Review and Activity

Chapter 14 · Buses and Interconnects

Buses and Interconnects

15.2 Ethernet, Wi-Fi, and IP Ethernet is widely used in wired LANs

Wi-Fi provides wireless LAN communication using radio. Both connect devices to local network infrastructure, but their performance and interference characteristics differ. IP supports logical addressing and routing. IPv4 uses 32-bit addresses, while IPv6 uses 128-bit addresses. Routers forward packets based on destination information. Network configuration may include an address, subnet prefix, default gateway, and DNS resolver. A device can be connected to a local network but still lack Internet access if routing, DNS, or upstream connectivity is unavailable.

15.3 Client-Server and Peer-to-Peer In client-server architecture, clients request services from servers

The server may host files, applications, databases, or APIs. In peer-to-peer systems, participating devices can act as both consumers and providers of resources. Client-server models centralize management and can simplify access control, but require server capacity and availability. Peer-to-peer designs can distribute load, though discovery, coordination, and security may be more complex. Many real systems are hybrids. For example, a service may use centralized authentication while transferring data directly between peers. Chapter 15 Review and Activity

Chapter 16 · Personal and Mobile Platforms

Personal and Mobile Platforms

Chapter 16 — Personal and Mobile Platforms Personal platforms include desktops, laptops, tablets, and smartphones. They are designed around user interaction, application support, and a balance of performance, portability, and cost. Mobile platforms place additional emphasis on energy efficiency, thermal limits, wireless connectivity, and sensors. A smartphone commonly integrates CPU cores, GPU, memory controller, modem, camera interfaces, audio, and security functions in an SoC. Integration helps reduce size and power consumption. Platform selection should reflect the intended activity. A mobile device may be ideal for communication and field work, while a workstation may better support demanding creation or scientific workloads.

16.1 Desktop and Laptop Systems Desktop systems often offer greater expandability, cooling capacity, and upgrade options

Laptops prioritize portability and integrate display, keyboard, battery, and wireless connectivity. Their thermal and power envelopes may limit sustained performance compared with larger systems. A platform specification should include more than a processor model: memory capacity, storage, graphics, display, ports, wireless capability, battery, and operating-system support all matter. For school or office use, maintainability and warranty can be important considerations. A well-matched computer can provide better real-world value than a more powerful system that exceeds the workload’s needs.

16.2 Mobile SoCs and Energy Mobile processors use power-management techniques such as dynamic voltag

e and frequency scaling, sleep states, and heterogeneous cores. Some cores are optimized for efficient background tasks, while others support demanding work. The operating system and hardware cooperate to balance performance and battery life.

Chapter 17 · Servers, Data Centers, and Cloud Platforms

Servers, Data Centers, and Cloud Platforms

Thermal design limits sustained operation. When a device becomes too hot, it may reduce frequency or power. This behavior is called thermal throttling and helps protect the device. Battery life depends on screen brightness, wireless activity, workload, battery health, and software behavior—not merely processor specifications.

16.3 Platform Ecosystems A platform ecosystem includes hardware vendors, operating systems, app stor

es or distribution channels, developer tools, services, and users. Ecosystems can provide convenience and integration, but may also introduce restrictions or dependency on particular vendors. Developers consider supported APIs, device diversity, security policies, and distribution requirements. Users consider compatibility, accessibility, privacy, updates, and long-term support. Interoperability standards and open formats can reduce lock-in and make it easier to move data between systems. Chapter 16 Review and Activity

Review questions

1. What platform needs are especially important for mobile devices? 2. What is an SoC? 3. Explain thermal throttling. 4. How do desktops and laptops differ in expandability? 5. What makes up a platform ecosystem? Activity Compare a laptop and smartphone for a student’s needs. Chapter 17 — Servers, Data Centers, and Cloud Platforms Servers provide shared services to users, applications, or other systems. They may host websites, databases, file services, authentication, analytics, or virtual machines. Server platforms emphasize capacity, reliability, remote administration, and efficient use of resources.

Chapter 17 · Servers, Data Centers, and Cloud Platforms

Servers, Data Centers, and Cloud Platforms

A data center houses computing, storage, networking, power, cooling, and physical security infrastructure. Cloud platforms provide computing resources through service interfaces, often with elastic provisioning and usage-based pricing. These environments scale from a single server to large distributed facilities.

17.1 Server Architecture and Reliability Servers may use multiple processors or cores, large memory

capacity, redundant power supplies, high-speed network interfaces, and error-detecting memory. Redundancy can reduce downtime, but adds cost and complexity. Reliability refers to the ability to operate correctly over time. Availability describes the proportion of time a service is usable. Fault tolerance allows a system to continue despite selected failures. Monitoring and maintenance are essential parts of server operations. A server is only as dependable as its complete system: hardware, software, network, power, cooling, and operational procedures.

17.2 Cloud Service Models Infrastructure as a Service (IaaS) offers virtualized compute, storage, and networking resources

Platform as a Service (PaaS) provides a managed environment for deploying applications. Software as a Service (SaaS) delivers complete applications to users. Cloud computing can reduce the need to purchase and maintain local infrastructure, and can support rapid scaling. It also introduces considerations such as recurring costs, data governance, connectivity, provider dependency, and shared-responsibility security models. Cloud adoption should be based on requirements and total cost over time, not on the assumption that cloud is always cheaper.

17.3 Scaling and Load Balancing Vertical scaling increases the resources of one system

Horizontal scaling adds more systems and distributes work among them. A load balancer directs requests across available servers and can support health checks or traffic policies.

Chapter 18 · Embedded Systems and IoT

Embedded Systems and IoT

Horizontal scaling may improve capacity and resilience, but applications must handle distributed state, communication delays, and partial failures. Stateless service components are often easier to scale, while databases and persistent state require careful design. Capacity planning estimates demand and identifies bottlenecks before users experience unacceptable performance. Chapter 17 Review and Activity

What does a load balancer do? Activity Design a basic hosting plan for a school information portal. Chapter 18 — Embedded Systems and IoT An embedded system is a computer designed to perform a specific function within a larger product. Examples include appliance controllers, vehicle systems, medical instruments, industrial equipment, and smart sensors. Embedded platforms may have strict limits on cost, memory, power, and physical size. The Internet of Things (IoT) connects sensors, actuators, and embedded devices to local or remote services. IoT systems commonly include device hardware, firmware, communication, gateways, cloud or edge processing, and user interfaces. Because embedded devices may operate unattended, reliability and security are especially important.

18.1 Microcontrollers and Real-Time Systems A microcontroller integrates a processor core, memory, a

nd peripheral interfaces for control tasks. It may run bare-metal firmware or a real-time operating system. A

Chapter 18 · Embedded Systems and IoT

Embedded Systems and IoT

microprocessor typically relies on external components for a broader computing platform, though modern terminology varies. Real-time systems are defined by timing requirements. A hard real-time system must meet critical deadlines; a soft real-time system can tolerate occasional deadline misses with reduced quality. Predictability can matter more than peak throughput. Designers analyze worst-case execution time, interrupt latency, scheduling, and resource limits to support timing guarantees.

18.2 Sensors, Actuators, and Connectivity Sensors measure conditions such as temperature, motion, pressure, or light

Actuators produce actions, such as moving a motor, opening a valve, or switching a relay. Analog signals may require conversion to digital values using an analog-to-digital converter. Embedded devices communicate using interfaces such as I²C, SPI, UART, Ethernet, Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, or low-power radio protocols. The appropriate choice depends on distance, throughput, power, complexity, and environment. A complete design includes calibration, error handling, safe operating limits, and a plan for updates.

18.3 IoT Security and Lifecycle IoT security begins with secure device identity, protected credentia

ls, authenticated communication, and restricted services. Devices should receive signed updates where possible and avoid hard-coded shared secrets. Physical access and supply-chain risks may also matter. A device lifecycle includes provisioning, deployment, monitoring, updates, repair, and retirement. Unsupported devices can become security liabilities. Data minimization and privacy should be considered when sensors collect information about people or their environment. A connected device is part of a larger system; securing only the cloud service is insufficient. Chapter 18 Review and Activity

Chapter 18 · Embedded Systems and IoT

Embedded Systems and IoT

A container image packages an application and its dependencies in a reusable format. A container runtime creates and manages running containers. Containers share the host kernel but use isolation mechanisms such as namespaces and resource controls in common implementations. Containers support consistent deployment across compatible environments. They can start quickly and use fewer resources than a full VM. However, kernel compatibility and security boundaries must be understood. Images should be maintained, scanned, and built from trusted sources. Secrets should not be embedded in image layers.

19.3 Virtualization Use Cases Virtualization supports server consolidation, development sandboxes, t

est environments, disaster recovery, and cloud infrastructure. Containers support microservices, continuous integration, and application packaging. A system may combine both: containers running inside VMs on cloud hosts. Operational success requires observability, network policy, identity controls, backup, patching, and capacity management. Virtual resources remain dependent on physical infrastructure. A useful design evaluates both technical fit and the skills required to manage the environment. Chapter 19 Review and Activity

Chapter 20 · Performance, Security, and Emerging Architectures

Performance, Security, and Emerging Architectures

Chapter 20 — Performance, Security, and Emerging Architectures Modern platform design must balance performance, energy, security, reliability, and cost. A system’s bottleneck may be CPU execution, memory latency, storage I/O, network capacity, or software coordination. Measuring the workload helps determine where improvement is useful. Security is a platform-wide concern. Hardware protections, firmware, operating-system controls, application practices, and operational policies work together. A weakness in one layer can undermine others. Emerging architectures include specialized accelerators, chiplet designs, edge computing, and experimental quantum systems. Each addresses particular workloads or design constraints rather than replacing all general-purpose computing.

20.1 Performance Evaluation Performance evaluation uses measurements and representative workloads

Common measures include response time, throughput, utilization, latency, and energy per task. A benchmark should be repeatable and disclose the environment and workload. Amdahl’s law illustrates the limits of accelerating only part of a program: the unchanged portion constrains total speedup. This reinforces the importance of profiling and identifying the dominant cost. Avoid drawing conclusions from a single metric. A system with high peak throughput may provide poor response time for interactive work.

20.2 Platform Security Foundations Platform security includes secure boot, firmware integrity, privi

lege separation, memory protection, encryption, identity management, and timely updates. Secure boot can help verify that startup components are trusted. Hardware security features may protect keys or support isolation. Security is not achieved by one feature. Configuration, software quality, patch management, backups, user behavior, and incident response all contribute. Threat modeling identifies assets, likely attackers, and potential attack paths.

Chapter 20 · Performance, Security, and Emerging Architectures

Performance, Security, and Emerging Architectures

The principle of least privilege gives each component only the permissions it needs. Defense in depth uses multiple independent safeguards.

20.3 Accelerators and New Directions Graphics processing units (GPUs) provide many parallel executio

n resources and are useful for graphics, scientific workloads, and machine learning. Other accelerators may target video processing, cryptography, or neural-network operations. Efficient use depends on software support and data movement. Chiplet designs combine smaller dies into one package, potentially improving manufacturing flexibility and integration. Edge computing places processing closer to data sources to reduce latency or bandwidth use. Quantum computing uses different physical principles and may benefit selected problem classes, but it is not a general replacement for classical systems. Emerging technologies should be evaluated by practical capability, maturity, cost, and workload fit. Chapter 20 Review and Activity
